approaches.name: (a) direct interpretation of the pattern string, recursive backtracking (Kernighan/Pike lineage + classes, |, (), {n,m}, lazy, UTF-8, icase)
approaches.description: No compile step: the pattern bytes are the program. Sequence matcher match(re,s,frame) loops over atoms and only recurses at choice points. Groups/alternation: on '(' a 24-byte frame_t {up, body, after, istart, count, min, max, lazy, capidx} is built on the C stack (closing ')' found by grp_end(): skip escapes, classes and nested groups; quantifier after ')' parsed into min/max/lazy; capture index = count of capturing '(' from pattern start, no table). The sequence matcher stops at ')' '|' or NUL = end of its alternative and calls done(): top level -> record match end; inside a frame -> one iteration of that group is complete: set capture (restore on failure), then rep() decides in priority order (greedy: run body again via alts() then continue after the group with the parent frame; lazy: reverse) subject to count<max, count>=min and the empty-iteration rule (an iteration that consumed nothing and count>=min may not loop again). alts() tries each '|' alternative by re-scanning to the next '|' at depth 0 (alt_end). Single-code-point atoms (literal, ., [..], \d\w\s): greedy = consume up to max iteratively, then back off one code point at a time (prev_cp) calling match() on the rest; lazy = try rest, then consume one. This is exactly Kernighan's matchstar shape (Beautiful Code ch.1: shortest-first loop, and his leftmost-longest variant that counts forward then backs off), generalised: the 'rest of pattern after the group' is simply frame->after and the enclosing frame->up. subreg (read) uses the same skip-to-'|'/')' idea (skip_block) but is possessive (no backtracking into repetitions) and anchored-only, which is why it fails general patterns. Search = for each start code point, alts(pat,s,NULL); first success wins (leftmost-first).
approaches.expected_code_size: MEASURED spike (all required features + \b\B + step budget), arm-none-eabi-gcc 10.3 -Os Cortex-M4: text=1886 B, data=0, bss=0 (Cortex-M0+ 1886; x86-64 clang 3400). Per function: match 760, atom 330, quant 196, rep 164, dre_search 140, alt_end 84, named_class 74, decode 64, class_end 42, is_word 32. Feature costs by #ifdef removal: \b\B 106 B, icase 70 B, {n,m} 134 B, step budget 34 B, UTF-8 144 B; all five removed = 1406 B. Compiler variance on the same file: gcc -O2 2196, -O1 2210, -O0 3310; Apple clang 21 thumbv7em -Os 2454 / -Oz 2176; -fno-inline +66 B; -fno-jump-tables/-fno-tree-switch-conversion 0 B. Estimate after size tuning (fold quant() into match, drop \b if not required, share range test): 1.6-1.8 KB. Correctness: passes 2080/2081 (corpus_seed1) and 3080/3081 (corpus_seed7) of the protocol difftest; the single failure in each is ^(a+)+$ on 27 a's+b which exhausts the 5M-step budget and reports error instead of nomatch.
approaches.ram_and_stack: Heap 0, static 0. State struct dre_t = 2*MAXCAP pointers + 5 words (MAXCAP=16: 152 B, caller-owned). Stack (gcc -fstack-usage, Cortex-M4 -Os): match 88 B, rep 64 B (holds a 24-byte frame_t), atom 40, quant 28, dre_search 40. Recursion grows by one match()+rep()+done() chain (~230 B) per group iteration on the current path and by one match() (88 B) per quantified atom whose continuation is being tried (the repetition itself is iterative). Typical short patterns/texts: 0.5-2 KB; worst case (a)* over an N-char text: ~230*N B. Needs a depth cap or step budget (both cheap: 34 B). Explicit-stack variant (c) is the fix if 1-2 KB C stacks are the norm.
approaches.worst_case: Exponential time (Cox regexp1: a?^n a^n needs O(2^n) with backtracking); ^(a+)+$ on 27 a's blows the 5M-step budget (Python's own backtracker is also exponential there). Mitigation options: step budget (34 B, deterministic error), depth limit, or BitState memoisation (RE2, regexp3: bitmap of visited (pc,sp) pairs, 'used when the bitmap is at most 32 kilobytes') - only valid if (pattern offset, text offset) determines the outcome, which fails with {n,m} counters unless counts are saturated in the key. No infinite loops: empty-iteration rule + every atom consumes >=1 code point.
approaches.hard_features: Easiest of all approaches for {n,m} (counter lives in the frame; 134 B total incl. parsing), lazy on groups (one flag, order of two calls), nested groups (frame->up chain), captures in repeated groups (set on iteration end / restore on failure = Python/Perl keep-last semantics; JS reset-per-iteration would need a loop over inner capture slots, ~30 B), UTF-8 negated classes (atom() decodes one code point before any test, so negation is one XOR). Awkward: (1) pattern is re-scanned on every group entry and alternative (alt_end/grp_end/cap_index) - harmless for speed here but means malformed patterns are detected late; a separate validate pass costs ~100-200 B; (2) the greedy back-off needs prev_cp (14 B) because positions are not stored; (3) recursion depth is data-dependent.
approaches.references: Kernighan, 'A Regular Expression Matcher' (Beautiful Code ch.1) + exercises, https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spr09/cos333/beautiful.html (fetched; quotes matchstar and the leftmost-longest variant); Kernighan & Pike TPOP ch.9 grep.c https://www.cs.princeton.edu/~bwk/tpop.webpage/grep.c (fetched); subreg source https://github.com/mattbucknall/subreg (cloned/read: skip_block, parse_repetition possessive loop, README 'Matches are greedy and possessive', 'Only supports anchored expressions'); spike /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-boogie-Workspace-mini-regexp/980e397c-0a6d-407c-9809-54b70c85e624/scratchpad/spikes/dre/dre.c

approaches.name: (b) compile to compact bytecode, then recursive backtracking (re1.5 recursiveloop style)
approaches.description: Parser emits a byte program (re1.5.h: Char c, Any, Class/ClassNot n pairs, NamedClass, Bol, Eol, Jmp off, Split off, RSplit off, Save n, Match; 8-bit relative offsets). Matcher is one loop+switch that recurses only at Split/RSplit (first branch, then fall through to second) and at Save (write slot, recurse, restore on failure) - re1.5/recursiveloop.c. Priority/greediness is the operand order of Split (Cox regexp2: e* = 'L1: split L2, L3' prefers e; e*? = 'L1: split L3, L2'); alternation = split L1,L2; L1: e1; jmp L3; L2: e2 (re1.5 compilecode.c inserts the split with memmove INSERT_CODE and patches the jmp). Counted repetition must be expanded at compile time (re1.5 README TODO: '{n} and {n,m}' unsupported) or needs counter instructions with a counter stack. re1.5 two-pass sizing: 'Exact size of the bytecode can be found prior to compilation' (README).
approaches.expected_code_size: MEASURED re1.5 (Cortex-M4 gcc 10.3 -Os): compilecode.c 1102 B (parser+emitter+sizecode) + recursiveloop.c 336 B + charclass.c 126 B = 1564 B WITHOUT {n,m}, UTF-8, icase, \b, and without empty-loop protection. Adding {n,m} by expansion (copying the term's bytecode n times, 16-bit offsets) ~150-250 B, UTF-8 (decoder in matcher + code-point class bounds) ~150 B (cf. 144 B in the spike), icase ~70 B: ESTIMATE 1.95-2.1 KB, i.e. ~150-250 B more than (a) and at the top of / above the 2 KB budget. The parser is the expensive part (1102 B for a subset).
approaches.ram_and_stack: Bytecode buffer (caller-provided; 5-byte search prefix + Save 0/1 + ~1-3 B per pattern atom; {n,m} expansion multiplies the term) + capture array (nsub*4 B). Stack: recursiveloop frame 48 B (measured) per Split/Save taken on the current path (~ number of choice points, ~text length for a* loops); no heap in compilecode/recursiveloop (re1.5's pike/backtrack matchers do use mal()).
approaches.worst_case: Exponential time like (a). Additionally (a*)* compiles to an epsilon loop 'L1: split L2,L3; L2: split L4,L1; ...' that recurses forever/overflows the stack unless a progress check is added (Cox regexp2: 'regular expressions like (a*)* can cause infinite loops in the compiled program'); re1.5 has no guard. Guard = record sp at loop entry (extra instruction or per-loop slot) ~40-80 B.
approaches.hard_features: {n,m}: expansion blows up bytecode and breaks 8-bit offsets (need 16-bit); lazy {n,m}? expands to nested RSplits; empty-match loops need an explicit progress instruction; captures inside repeated groups are fine (Save with restore); nested groups fine; UTF-8: Class operands become code points (3 B per bound or varint) and Char c becomes a multi-byte compare; error handling: re1.5 returns codes but e.g. 'nothing to repeat' and unbalanced ')' are only partly checked.
approaches.references: Cox, 'Regular Expression Matching: the Virtual Machine Approach' https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp2.html (fetched); re1.5 README/compilecode.c/recursiveloop.c/re1.5.h https://github.com/pfalcon/re1.5 (cloned, read, measured); re1 https://github.com/rsc/re1 (cloned)

approaches.name: (c) bytecode + backtracking with an explicit thread stack (re1/re1.5 backtrack.c)
approaches.description: Same bytecode as (b); on Split push (pc, sp, captures) onto a fixed array and continue the preferred branch; on failure pop. LIFO order reproduces recursion priority (Cox regexp2: 'Because the threads are managed in a stack (last in, first out), the thread for pc->y will not execute until all threads created by pc->x have been tried and failed'). Captures per pushed thread must be snapshotted: re1.5 uses refcounted copy-on-write Sub objects (sub.c: newsub/incref/update/decref + mal()); the MCU-friendly alternative is an undo log (push (slot, old value) records on the same stack, 4-6 B per Save) instead of copying all slots.
approaches.expected_code_size: MEASURED re1.5 backtrack.c 477 B vs recursiveloop.c 336 B (+141 B) plus sub.c 126 B for the refcounted captures = +267 B over (b)'s matcher; with the same compiler (1102) and charclass (126): 1831 B before {n,m}/UTF-8/icase -> ESTIMATE 2.1-2.4 KB. Marginal cost of the explicit stack itself ~150-250 B.
approaches.ram_and_stack: Deterministic: C stack is flat (re1.5's frame is 12,048 B only because of 'enum { MAX = 1000 }; Thread ready[MAX]' with 12-byte Threads - shrink to 32-64 entries of (pc 2 B, sp 2 B) + undo records = 256-512 B, overflow is a clean error). Bytecode buffer as in (b). This is the main advantage over (a)/(b) on MCUs with 1-4 KB stacks.
approaches.worst_case: Exponential time (same search space as (a)/(b)); stack overflow becomes a reported error instead of a crash. Empty-loop hazard identical to (b).
approaches.hard_features: Captures inside repeated groups (snapshot vs undo log is the whole design question); {n,m} counters must live in the thread record or be expanded; lazy = operand order (free); nested groups fine; UTF-8 same as (b).
approaches.references: Cox regexp2 (backtrackingvm, 'ready[MAXTHREAD]'); re1.5/backtrack.c, re1.5/sub.c (read, measured, -fstack-usage 12048 B)

approaches.name: (d) Pike VM / Thompson NFA simulation with fixed-size thread lists
approaches.description: Same bytecode; run all threads in lock step over the input. Thread = pc (+ its own capture array). addthread() follows Jmp/Split/Save/Bol/Eol immediately and marks visited pcs per step (re1.5 sets bit 0x80 in the opcode byte) so 'only one thread per PC needs to be kept' (Cox regexp2); leftmost-first priority is preserved by adding threads in Split order and cutting the list at the first Match. Captures are copied per thread ('memmove(saved, t.saved, sizeof t.saved)'); re1.5 reduces copying with refcounted copy-on-write Subs, which needs an allocator.
approaches.expected_code_size: MEASURED re1.5 pike.c 680 B (pikevm 396 + addthread 284) + sub.c 126 + cleanmarks ~30 vs recursiveloop 336: matcher is ~+500 B over (b); with the compiler 1102 + charclass 126 = ~2.06 KB before {n,m}/UTF-8/icase -> ESTIMATE 2.3-2.7 KB. Cannot fit 2 KB with the required feature set unless the compiler is made much smaller than re1.5's.
approaches.ram_and_stack: Bounded and known at compile time: two thread lists of length nprog, each entry pc (2 B) + captures (2*ncap*2 B) -> 64-instruction program with 10 captures = 2*64*42 = 5.4 KB, vs a few hundred bytes for (a)/(c). addthread recursion 112 B/frame (measured), depth = length of epsilon chains. {n,m} by expansion enlarges nprog and therefore both lists.
approaches.worst_case: O(n*m) time guaranteed (Cox regexp1/2), no exponential blow-up, no infinite loops on (a*)* (dedup by pc). The only approach that removes the step-budget/hang risk entirely.
approaches.hard_features: {n,m}: expansion only (a{1,100} = 100 copies; no counters without state explosion); captures = the dominant code+RAM cost (per-thread arrays); lazy is free (Split order); \b needs a look-back byte in addthread (fine); UTF-8 fine (one step per code point); nested/empty loops fine.
approaches.references: Cox regexp1 https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp1.html and regexp2 (fetched); re1.5/pike.c, re1/pike.c (read, measured)

approaches.name: (e) lazy DFA (RE2-style)
approaches.description: Build DFA states (sets of NFA states) on demand from the compiled NFA and cache them (Cox regexp1: 'caches the Lists in spare memory ... essentially computing the equivalent DFA as it is needed'; regexp3: 'If the cache fills, the DFA frees them all and starts over'). Requires everything in (b)'s compiler plus state-set hashing, a transition cache in RAM, and a reverse DFA or a second engine to recover match start and submatches (regexp3: DFA answers match/where, then 'invoke the NFA to find submatch boundaries'; RE2 falls back to OnePass/BitState/NFA for captures).
approaches.expected_code_size: Not measured; by construction > (d) + hashing/cache management: well above 3 KB even minimal, and it still cannot deliver the required features (see below).
approaches.ram_and_stack: Unbounded/cache-managed: a DFA state = one NFA state set (nprog bits) + up to 256 (or per-class) transitions; RE2 budgets megabytes. Exactly the resource an MCU lacks.
approaches.worst_case: Linear per byte if cached, but state explosion ((((a*)*)*)...) forces cache flushes; captures need a second pass anyway.
approaches.hard_features: Does not fit: no captures, no greedy/lazy distinction (a DFA only knows the set of live states, not priority), leftmost-first submatch semantics need the NFA/backtracker, and {n,m} expansion multiplies the state space. Only worth it when speed on long inputs matters - explicitly not the case here.
approaches.references: Cox, 'Regular Expression Matching in the Wild' https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp3.html (fetched); regexp1 (fetched)

size_tricks: Dispatch shape (measured tricks.c, gcc 10.3 -Os Thumb-2): dense 12-way switch on 0..11 -> TBB jump table 86 B; equivalent if-chain 108 B; switch on 12 sparse ASCII metachars 122 B (compare chain). Bytecode engines get the table for free by numbering opcodes densely; a direct interpreter pays ~+40% for dispatch, so order tests by frequency and share tails (the spike's match() is 760 B, of which dispatch is a minor part).

Computed class predicates beat tables: c-'0'<10 = 12 B, space test 20 B, word test 32 B; ONE function for \d\s\w incl. negation-by-uppercase = 76 B, versus a 128-byte flag table + 28 B lookup = 156 B. A 16-byte bitmap membership test costs 26 B of code (only worthwhile for precompiled irregular sets). Never use ctype (pulls a 257-byte table + locale plumbing).

Share one 'test one code point' routine (atom()) among literal, '.', [...] and \d\w\s, and reuse the named-class function inside brackets so [\d\s] is free; put icase folding in that one place (whole icase feature = 70 B measured).
Unsigned-compare range idiom c - lo <= hi - lo (one SUBS+CMP) for ranges, classes and digit/letter tests; keep everything unsigned 32-bit (uint32_t code points, uint16_t counters with INF=0xFFFF).
No 64-bit arithmetic: u64 mul+shift 28 B vs u32 8 B, u64 compare 14 B, and any u64 divide pulls __aeabi_uldivmod (~hundreds of bytes from libgcc, invisible in the .o).
No varargs (va_list loop 32 B vs pointer loop 18 B, plus per-call-site marshalling) and no printf-family anywhere in the engine; report errors as small integers.
Bit-flags packed in one byte: 8 B to test four flags vs 22 B for four ints (and 3 B vs 16 B of RAM).
Zero libc: take (ptr,len), hand-roll strlen (16 B)/memcpy (20 B) if needed at all; the spike includes only <stdint.h>/<stddef.h>. A bl to libc is 4 B in the .o but links kilobytes.

Let gcc inline: all helpers static; -fno-inline costs +66 B on the spike, -fno-inline-functions-called-once +6 B. Do not hand-inline either: a 4-arg leaf costs ~12-14 B per call site (arg marshal + bl) + 12 B body; three calls = 52 B vs 36 B inlined - so inline only when the body is tiny or called once.

Argument passing: keep hot recursive functions at <=4 register args (AAPCS r0-r3); a state-struct pointer is not automatically smaller (rec_struct 66 B vs 6 loose args 56 B in the microbench) - it wins only when >4 args would spill at every call site or fields are read many times.

Only recurse at choice points; concatenation is a loop with continue (the spike's match() loop). Recursion frames are 40-90 B each on Thumb-2 (-fstack-usage), so this is a RAM trick as much as a code trick.
Counted repetition as an integer counter in the repetition state (134 B for full {n},{n,},{n,m},{,m} incl. parsing) instead of pattern/bytecode expansion.
Always include a step budget (34 B) or depth limit; it is far cheaper than any memoisation and turns catastrophic patterns into an error code.
UTF-8: minimal non-validating decoder 64 B, skip-only 18 B, backward step 14 B; validating decoder 140 B - do not validate inside the matcher (whole UTF-8 support in the spike 144 B).

Compiler/flags: -Os (1886) vs -O2 2196 / -O1 2210 / -O0 3310; gcc 10.3 -Os beat Apple clang 21 -Oz (2176) by 13% and clang -Os (2454) by 23% on the same file; -fno-jump-tables, -fno-tree-switch-conversion, -mslow-flash-data: 0 B change; -mno-unaligned-access +10 B. Always -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections + --gc-sections and a 1-2 function public API so unused entry points vanish.

rodata is flash too: the protocol's 'text' already includes .rodata; a table pays off only for sets with more than ~8 ranges. Keep error strings out entirely (re1.5's fatal() strings cost 29 B in backtrack.c alone).

Pattern-as-program (approach a) is itself the biggest trick: it deletes the parser/emitter (re1.5's compilecode.c alone is 1102 B, more than half of any bytecode design's budget) and the bytecode RAM buffer.
semantics_notes:
'Modern basics' = the Perl/JS/Python backtracking family: LEFTMOST-FIRST (ordered) semantics, not POSIX leftmost-longest. perlre: 'the first alternative found for which the entire expression matches, is the one that is chosen'; e.g. (a|ab)(c|bcd)(d*) on 'abcd' gives groups 'a','bcd','' (corpus/Python; the spike agrees) whereas POSIX subexpression rules give 'ab','cd',''. Greedy = as many as possible, lazy (*?, +?, ??, {n,m}?) = as few as possible, both by choice-point order (ECMAScript RepeatMatcher: 'If greedy is false, then Let z be continue(matchState). If z is not failure, return z. Return m(xr, d).'). EMPTY-MATCH LOOP RULE: ECMAScript RepeatMatcher: 'If min = 0 and y's [[EndIndex]] = matchState's [[EndIndex]], return failure' (Note 4: prevents the infinite loop on /(a*)*/); Perl ('Repeated Patterns Matching a Zero-length Substring') and Python instead ACCEPT one empty iteration and stop looping. Observable difference: JS /(a*)*/.exec('b') leaves group 1 undefined, Python/Perl give group 1 = '' at (0,0) (corpus hand case, Python oracle). CAPTURES IN REPEATED GROUPS: ECMAScript clears the atom's captures on every iteration ('Step 4 of the RepeatMatcher clears Atom's captures each time Atom is repeated': /(z)((a+)?(b+)?(c))*/.exec('zaacbbbcac') -> group 4 undefined), Perl/Python keep the last successful value (group 4 = 'bbb'); the corpus expects Python (keep-last), which is also the cheapest to implement. '$': Perl/Python match at end OR just before a final '
' (Python docs: 'Matches the end of the string or just before the newline at the end of the string'); JS (no /m) only at the very end. '.': all three exclude '
' (JS additionally , U+2028, U+2029; Python re.DOTALL/Perl /s flip it). '^' only at position 0 without multiline. \w = [A-Za-z0-9_] under Python re.ASCII, Perl /a, and JS always; \d = [0-9]; \s = [ 	
 \v] (Python ASCII); JS \s also matches Unicode spaces and U+FEFF, Perl \s includes \v since 5.18 - so 'ASCII \s = 6 chars' is the Python/JS-compatible choice.  /\B are derived from \w, so with ASCII \w a boundary fires inside 'héllo'. Class escapes: \d\w\s and their negations are allowed inside [...] in all three; escaped ] \ - ^ inside classes; a leading ']' is literal in Perl/Python but JS treats [] as an empty class - always accept the escaped form. {n}, {n,}, {n,m}; Python also {,m} (=0..m); an invalid brace ('a{', 'a{x}') is a literal '{' in Perl/Python/JS-nonunicode (error in JS /u). Errors: a**, a{1,2}{2} ('multiple repeat'), a{2,1}, *a, a|*, unbalanced ( or [ are errors in Python (the corpus only requires the engine not to hang on them). Case-insensitive: fold ASCII letters only; Python with re.ASCII folds 'only letters a-z and A-Z'; without re.ASCII Python/JS/Perl also fold Unicode (e.g. Kelvin sign) - out of scope. Match positions are byte offsets in UTF-8; Python's oracle spans are converted to bytes by the corpus generator.
utf8_notes: Cheapest correct scheme (measured in the spike): decode ONE code point per atom test with a 64-byte non-validating decoder (c=*p++; if(c>=0xC0){n=c>=0xF0?3:c>=0xE0?2:1; c&=0x3F>>n; while(n--) c=(c<<6)|(*p++&0x3F);}) shared by pattern literals, '.', class members/range bounds, negated classes and the search-start advance; a 14-byte backward step (while((*--s&0xC0)==0x80);) for the greedy back-off; total UTF-8 support = 144 B by #ifdef removal (1886 -> 1742). Negated classes are then free: the atom always consumes a whole code point before testing, so [^é] cannot match one byte of 'é' (the classic byte-wise bug in tiny-regex-c/re1.5) and '.' is one code point except '\n' (two compares). Range tests work on code point values, so [é-ű] is correct with no extra code; \d\w\s stay ASCII tests on the value (non-ASCII simply fails them). Case folding must be gated on ASCII letters ((c|0x20)-'a'<26) BEFORE flipping bit 5 - the corpus caught the spike matching 'ő' (U+0151) against 'ű' (U+0171) under /i; the fix is 6 bytes. Validation: a validating decoder is 140 B (2.2x) and needs an error policy; for a scripting host whose strings are already valid UTF-8, don't validate, but guarantee no out-of-bounds read (check s<end before each atom and rely on a NUL/padding byte or clamp the continuation loop on end). Do not precompile classes to bitmaps (code space is 0x110000); linear range scan per test is correct and tiny. Reporting byte offsets is natural (pointers); code-point offsets would need a counting pass.
isa_density: OWN MEASUREMENT (same C, same flags -Os -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections, strict sum of .text+.rodata+.literal): Xtensa LX6 (xtensa-esp32-elf-gcc 8.4.0, PlatformIO toolchain) = 0.94-1.31x the Thumb-2 size (arm-none-eabi-gcc 10.3), median ~1.12x [re.c 1.12, subreg 1.15, re1.5 backtrack 1.11, compilecode 1.17, pike 0.94, recursiveloop 1.12, charclass 1.31, tricks 1.29, dre spike 1.12]; with -mlongcalls, which ESP-IDF always passes, dre goes 2129 -> 2325 B = 1.23x Thumb-2. RV32IMC (riscv32-esp-elf-gcc 12.2.0, ESP32-C3/C6 class) = 1.26-1.45x, median ~1.37x [dre 1.27x, compilecode 1.45x]; RV32IM without the C extension = 1.65-1.99x (~1.85x), i.e. RVC saved 26-28% here, matching the RISC-V spec claim. So a 1.9 KB Thumb-2 engine is ~2.1-2.3 KB on ESP32 (Xtensa) and ~2.4-2.6 KB on ESP32-C3 (RISC-V); RISC-V is ~1.2x Xtensa on this code. Caveat: three different gcc majors (10.3 / 8.4 / 12.2); LX7 (ESP32-S3) uses the same 16/24-bit encodings as LX6, only LX6 was measured. LITERATURE: RISC-V ISA spec 20191213 ch.16 (PDF fetched, text verified): 'Typically, 50%-60% of the RISC-V instructions in a program can be replaced with RVC instructions, resulting in a 25%-30% code-size reduction'; the chapter also states the first-generation Thumb/MIPS16 and second-generation 'ARM Thumb2, microMIPS, PowerPC VLE' history but carries no cross-ISA figure. Perotti et al., 'HW/SW approaches for RISC-V code size reduction', CARRV 2020 (PDF fetched, https://carrv.github.io/2020/papers/CARRV2020_paper_12_Perotti.pdf), Table 1: ARM-Thumb2 209,696 B vs RV32IMC 233,628 B (+11.41%) on 3GPP IoT code and 1766 vs 1966 B (+11.33%) on Embench, GCC 7.x, -Os -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections, Cortex-M3 vs rv32imc; their push/pop extension cuts the gap to 7.7%/5.8%. Weaver & McKee, 'Code density concerns for new architectures', ICCD 2009 (PDF fetched, https://web.eece.maine.edu/~vweaver/papers/iccd09/iccd09_density.pdf): 21 ISAs hand-optimised, 'up to a factor of three difference in code sizes from ISA alone', and with compilers 'a factor of two in code density'; classic ARM Thumb is in their 16-bit 'embedded' group, Thumb-2/Xtensa/RISC-V are not measured (figure values are graphics, not extractable). UNVERIFIED (search snippets only; Berkeley servers refused every fetch): Waterman's MS thesis (UCB EECS-2011-63) reportedly puts Thumb-2 ~7% smaller than RVC on SPEC CPU2006 and 'the most optimal ARM solution ... is 99% of the RISC-V program using compressed instructions'. Xtensa vendor material (Cadence LX7 datasheet, search snippet) only claims '16- and 24-bit ... instruction encoding ... highly efficient code', no numbers; the esphome issue #9827 anecdote (RISC-V C3 firmware 'around twice the size' of Xtensa) compares different frameworks/libraries and is not a controlled measurement - my controlled ratio is 1.22x. arXiv 2510.04158 (Scry) contains no Thumb-2/Xtensa numbers (checked). MULTIPLIER RANGE to use: Thumb-2 1.0; Xtensa LX6/LX7 1.1-1.25 (1.25 with -mlongcalls); RV32IMC 1.1-1.45 (literature 1.11, this code 1.27-1.45); RV32IM (no C) 1.65-2.0.
